1044.title: Rose Philippine Duchesne (18 November)
1044.hook: a French sister who went west in America; the Potawatomi called her the woman who always prays
1044.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep the memorial of Saint Rose Philippine Duchesne on 18 November, and schools of the Society of the Sacred Heart mark her feast.

segments.voice: Last time, Gertrude the Great, who asked the beloved disciple about the heartbeats he heard. Your line was the heart. When did you pause with a hand on your chest? Day one thousand forty-four.

An old woman kneels in a small mission chapel on the Kansas prairie. She has come a long way to be here, and she can't speak the language of the people she came to serve. She tried, and it wouldn't stick. So she does the one thing left to her. She prays, for hours, in the chapel. The Potawatomi people of the mission watch her, and they give her a name. In English it's usually given as the woman who prays always. Today's word is the sister who couldn't teach in words, and taught anyway.
screen: `AN OLD WOMAN ON THE PRAIRIE.` → `SHE CAN'T LEARN THE LANGUAGE.` → `SO SHE PRAYS.`

segments.voice: Rose Philippine Duchesne was born in France, in Grenoble, to a well-off family. She became a nun young, lived through the upheaval of the French Revolution when convents were shut, and afterward joined a new religious order, the Society of the Sacred Heart, founded by Madeleine Sophie Barat to educate girls. From early on Philippine had a fixed dream: to go to America and teach the native peoples there. For years she asked. For years she was told to wait. When at last she was allowed to go, she crossed the ocean with a few sisters to the Mississippi valley and set up a school in Saint Charles, in Missouri. It was hard: cold, poverty, illness, and a new language she never mastered. She ran schools and convents for years, and much of it felt to her like failure. Then, when she was old and frail, the Jesuits asked for sisters at their mission among the Potawatomi at Sugar Creek in Kansas. Others thought she was too weak to go. A priest said, in effect, that she must come, because even if she could do little work, she would pray, and that would draw down blessings. So she went. And that's how she spent her time there: praying in the chapel. The story goes that children, curious, would put bits of paper on the hem of her habit while she knelt, and come back hours later to find them still there. It's Paul's line, taken at its word: "Pray without ceasing." Her dream had been to teach. What she gave them was a picture of prayer that they put into a name.
screen: `A FRENCH NUN WITH A FIXED DREAM.` · `YEARS OF WAITING, THEN AMERICA.` · `OLD AND FRAIL, TO SUGAR CREEK.` · `PAPER ON HER HEM.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: one extra time. Settle, and breathe. Think of the places your day already pauses: waking, a meal, a commute, a door you walk through. Choose one more pause than you usually keep, and set it in mind now. If you pray, you can pray then, with a line you already know, or in silence. If you don't, that extra pause can be a breath and a moment of attention. For now, kneel or sit as Philippine did, and stay still for two minutes, as if a scrap of paper were resting on your sleeve. The bell holds the time.
Rose Philippine Duchesne. A French sister of the Society of the Sacred Heart who taught in Missouri and prayed among the Potawatomi in Kansas.
Your line: she who always prays. Today, keep the one extra pause you chose, even for a few seconds, and let it stand where a word would have failed. Day one thousand forty-four.

1045.title: The Presentation of Mary (21 November)
1045.hook: tradition says Mary was brought to the Temple as a child
1045.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of the Presentation of the Blessed Virgin Mary on 21 November; some religious communities renew their vows on this day, and Orthodox Christians keep it as the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple.

segments.voice: Last time, Rose Philippine Duchesne, the sister on the prairie who prayed when words failed. Your line was she who always prays. Where did you keep your extra pause? Day one thousand forty-five.

A little girl stands at the steps of the Temple in Jerusalem. Her parents have brought her here to give her to God, as they promised. The priest takes her and sets her down on a step near the altar, and, the old story says, she dances on her feet, and the whole house of Israel loves her. The Bible never tells this scene. It comes from an old writing outside the Bible. But the Church keeps a feast for it today. Today's word is the child on the steps.
screen: `A CHILD AT THE TEMPLE STEPS.` → `SHE DANCES ON HER FEET.` → `NOT IN THE BIBLE.`

segments.voice: The story comes from a writing usually called the Protoevangelium of James, a telling of Mary's childhood that the Church never placed in the Bible but that shaped Christian prayer and art. In it, Mary's parents, Joachim and Anne, have no child for a long time. Anne promises that if God gives her one, the child will be given back to serve God. Mary is born. When she is three years old, the story says, they bring her to the Temple, with girls carrying lamps so she won't turn back, and she is raised there. That's the scene the feast remembers. Now the honest part. The Church doesn't ask anyone to treat the details as history. What it keeps is the meaning. The feast sees in Mary someone given to God from the very start, so that when the angel comes to her years later, her yes isn't a sudden thing. It grows out of a life already offered. And the story didn't come from nowhere. It echoes a story the Bible does tell. In the first book of Samuel, called the first book of Kings in the Douay Bible, Hannah has no child and prays in the house of the Lord. She promises that if God gives her a son, she'll give him back. Samuel is born, and when he's weaned she brings him to the house of the Lord and leaves him there to serve. Two mothers, two promises, two children given early. Orthodox Christians keep this day too, under the name of Mary's Entrance into the Temple. Whatever happened on those steps, both feasts hold the same picture: a child given as a child.
screen: `AN OLD WRITING OUTSIDE THE BIBLE.` · `GIVEN BACK, AS ANNE PROMISED.` · `THE MEANING, NOT THE DETAILS.` · `HANNAH AND SAMUEL BEFORE HER.` · then, large: `GIVEN AS A CHILD.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: hold the children in faith. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one child you know: a son or daughter, a niece, a godchild, a kid from down the street. Then the children being raised in faith anywhere: learning their first prayers, sitting through services they don't understand yet, asking questions nobody can answer. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or ask Mary to watch over them. If you don't, simply wish each one well, slowly, one at a time, for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The Presentation of Mary. The feast that remembers the old story of Mary, as a small child, brought to the Temple and given to God by her parents.
Your line: given as a child. Today, do one kind thing for a child, or for the child someone else still carries inside them, and do it without asking anything back. Day one thousand forty-five.

1046.title: Cecilia (22 November)
1046.hook: a Roman martyr, patron of musicians
1046.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Cecilia on 22 November, and choirs, organists and music schools sometimes mark her feast with a concert or a sung Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Presentation of Mary, the old story of a child at the Temple steps. Your line was given as a child. What kind thing did you do for a child? Day one thousand forty-six.

A wedding in Rome. The house is loud with instruments, guests are eating and laughing, and the bride sits in the middle of it all. The old account of her life says that while the music played, she was singing too. But not out loud. She was singing in her heart, to God alone, asking to stay true to him. Nobody at the party could hear a note of it. That bride is Cecilia, and the silent song is why musicians, choirs and organists claim her as their patron. Today's word is the woman whose song nobody heard.
screen: `A LOUD WEDDING IN ROME.` → `THE BRIDE SINGS IN SILENCE.` → `THE PATRON OF MUSICIANS.`

segments.voice: Cecilia is one of the martyrs of Rome named in the old Roman Canon of the Mass. Her story comes from an old account of her martyrdom that reads more like a legend than a record, so it's best told as what tradition says. Tradition says she was a Christian woman of a noble family, promised in marriage to a young man named Valerian. On the wedding night she told him that an angel of God watched over her. Valerian wanted to see the angel. She sent him to a bishop named Urban, and he came back baptized. Then his brother Tiburtius came to believe too. In time the brothers were put to death for their faith, and then Cecilia. The account says even her death was slow, and that she kept speaking of God and giving away what she had until the end. Now the music. The Church's old prayer for her feast has a line in Latin, cantantibus organis: while the instruments were playing. The full line says that while they played, Cecilia sang in her heart to the Lord alone. In the old account, the instruments are the wedding music around her, the music she wasn't listening to. Over time, people heard the line the other way round, and Cecilia became the saint of the instruments themselves: of organs and choirs, of anyone who makes music. Both readings land in the same place. The song that mattered was the one inside, the one no guest could hear. In her story, music can be a prayer, and so can silence under the music.
screen: `A MARTYR NAMED IN THE ROMAN CANON.` · `VALERIAN AND THE ANGEL.` · `WHILE THE INSTRUMENTS PLAYED.` · `PATRON OF ALL WHO MAKE MUSIC.` · then, large: `SHE SANG IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Today's practice: sing or play something. If you can, hum a tune you know, quietly, or tap a rhythm on the table, or pick up an instrument. If you're somewhere you can't make a sound, do what Cecilia did: let the tune run in your head, note by note. Settle, and breathe first. Then give the music two minutes of full attention. If you pray, you can make the song a prayer, a hymn you know, or a psalm. If you don't, simply let one piece of music have all of you for a while. The bell holds the time.
Cecilia. A martyr of Rome who, tradition says, sang in her heart to God while the wedding music played, and the patron of musicians.
Your line: she sang in her heart. Today, in the loudest place you find yourself, keep one quiet tune running inside you. Day one thousand forty-six.

1047.title: Columban (23 November)
1047.hook: an Irish monk who founded monasteries across Europe
1047.howItsDone: Saint Columban is remembered on 23 November, with particular devotion in Ireland and at the places his monasteries stood, such as Luxeuil in France and Bobbio in Italy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cecilia, the Roman martyr musicians call their own. Your line was she sang in her heart. Did you sing or play something, even quietly? Day one thousand forty-seven.

A small boat pushes off from the Irish coast. In it sits a monk named Columban with a few companions. Nobody is chasing them. No bishop has sent them away. They are leaving on purpose, and they are not planning a return trip. The monk who later wrote Columban's life, Jonas of Bobbio, tells how he crossed the sea and walked into the kingdoms of the Franks, a stranger in a country where he knew no one. He found wild, half-empty hills and started building. Today, a man who made his home out of being away from home.
screen: `A BOAT LEAVES IRELAND.` → `NO ONE SENT THEM.` → `A STRANGER BUILDS IN THE HILLS.`

segments.voice: Columban's leaving had a pattern behind it, and the pattern is old. In Genesis, God's call to Abram is a hard one. In the Douay-Rheims: "Go forth out of thy country, and from thy kindred." No map. Just go. The letter to the Hebrews looks back on Abraham and the others who lived in tents and says they confessed that they were "pilgrims and strangers on the earth." Some Irish monks took that line personally. They spoke of a pilgrimage for Christ: leaving your own people, not for a holiday and not for a shrine, but as an offering, with the road itself as the prayer. Columban lived it. In the hills of Gaul he founded monasteries, Annegray and then Luxeuil, and people came to join him. He wrote a rule for his monks, strict and short. He also made enemies. Jonas tells how a king's household asked him to bless the king's sons, born outside the king's marriage, and Columban refused. The quarrel ended with him ordered out of the kingdom. So he kept walking. He crossed the Alps into Italy, and at Bobbio he founded one more monastery, and there his road ended. A tourist goes for the view and comes home. A pilgrim of this kind lets the unfamiliar place strip things away: the habits, the reputation, the comfortable chair. Columban never kept a comfortable chair for long.
screen: `GO FORTH OUT OF THY COUNTRY.` · `PILGRIMS AND STRANGERS ON THE EARTH.` · `LUXEUIL, THEN EXILE, THEN BOBBIO.` · `A PILGRIM LETS THE ROAD CHANGE HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be a pilgrim for two minutes. Get up and go somewhere you don't usually sit. A different chair. The back step. A window you rarely look out of. The far corner of the room. Settle there and notice that the place feels a little strange. Let that strangeness wake you up. If you pray, you can offer this new spot to God, the way Abram was told to go to a land he would be shown. If you don't, simply notice what you can see from here that you never see from your usual seat. The bell holds the time.
Columban. The Irish monk who left home on purpose, planted monasteries from Gaul to Italy, and treated being a stranger as his way of following Christ.
Your line: pilgrim for christ. Today, take a different route somewhere you go every day, and let the unfamiliar street be part of your prayer. Day one thousand forty-seven.

1048.title: Miguel Pro (23 November)
1048.hook: a Mexican Jesuit shot with his arms stretched out, saying long live Christ the King
1048.howItsDone: Blessed Miguel Agustín Pro is remembered on 23 November in some local calendars, including in Mexico and the United States, and Catholics there often pray for those who suffer for their faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Columban, the Irish monk who left home on purpose. Your line was pilgrim for christ. Did you take a different road somewhere? Day one thousand forty-eight.

A yard in Mexico City. A wall. A line of men with rifles. A priest in a plain suit is walked out to stand in front of them. According to the accounts handed down, he asks for one thing: a moment to pray. He kneels. He prays. Then he gets up, and instead of folding his hands or bracing himself, he stretches his arms out wide, the shape of a cross, and says a few words in Spanish. Those words are today's line. The man is Miguel Pro.
screen: `A YARD, A WALL, A LINE OF RIFLES.` → `HE KNEELS TO PRAY.` → `ARMS STRETCHED WIDE.`

segments.voice: Miguel Pro was a Jesuit priest at a time when the Mexican government had turned hard against the Church. Public worship stopped. Priests who stayed did their work in secret. Pro stayed. The stories told about him are full of disguises: a mechanic in overalls, a beggar, a well-dressed young man strolling past the police. He said Mass in private houses, heard confessions, and carried communion to people who couldn't get to a church. The stories are also full of jokes; he seems to have been funny, even in hiding. Then came a failed attack on a former president, and Pro and his brothers were arrested. The accounts say he had no part in it, and that he was shot without a trial. Now look at his last moment, because it was a prayer made with the body. He knelt first. Then he stood with his arms out. The posture is the shape of the cross. And the accounts say he forgave the men in front of him, which echoes what Jesus says from the cross in Luke's gospel. In the Douay-Rheims: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." The accounts give his last words as the cry of persecuted Catholics in Mexico in those years: viva Cristo Rey. Long live Christ the King. It isn't a curse on anyone. It's a statement about who rules. The soldiers held the rifles; he named a different king. The Church declared him blessed, and in some places his day is kept on 23 November, close to the feast of Christ the King.
screen: `A PRIEST IN HIDING, IN DISGUISE.` · `ARRESTED, SHOT WITHOUT A TRIAL.` · `ARMS OUT: A PRAYER MADE WITH THE BODY.` · `HE NAMED A DIFFERENT KING.` · then, large: `VIVA CRISTO REY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray with your arms. Stand or sit up straight. Slowly stretch your arms out to the sides, palms open, as wide as feels easy. Hold them there while you take a few slow breaths, and notice how open, and how unprotected, the body feels. When your arms tire, lower them and rest your hands on your knees, palms up. If you pray, you can say the three words, viva Cristo Rey, quietly, once. If you don't, just stay with the open hands. The bell holds the time.
Miguel Pro. The Jesuit who served in disguise while churches were closed, and who died with his arms out, naming Christ as King.
Your line: viva cristo rey. Today, when something tries to run your whole mood, open your hands for a second, the way he did, and let it go by. Day one thousand forty-eight.

1049.title: Catherine of Alexandria (25 November)
1049.hook: a learned martyr of legend, patron of students and philosophers
1049.howItsDone: Saint Catherine of Alexandria is remembered on 25 November; schools, colleges and student groups named for her sometimes mark the day, and art shows her with a book and a broken wheel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Miguel Pro, who died with his arms stretched wide. Your line was viva cristo rey. Did you open your hands at some point? Day one thousand forty-nine.

What would you do if an emperor called in his cleverest philosophers to argue you out of your faith, in public, with your life on the line? That's the scene at the heart of today's story. A young woman of Alexandria, well read and well born, walks up to the emperor and tells him his persecution is wrong. He doesn't have her killed on the spot. He does something stranger. He sends for the experts. Let's see who wins. Today, Catherine of Alexandria.
screen: `A YOUNG WOMAN FACES AN EMPEROR.` → `HE SENDS FOR THE EXPERTS.` → `WHO WINS THE ARGUMENT?`

segments.voice: First, an honest word about the source. Catherine's story reaches us as a legend, a martyr's tale told and retold, and historians can't confirm its details. The Church keeps her feast on 25 November and leaves that question open. What the legend gives us is a picture worth looking at. In the story, the philosophers arrive ready to make short work of a girl. Catherine argues back, point by point. And the debate ends the wrong way for the emperor: the philosophers themselves come over to her side, and they are put to death for it. Then the emperor tries to break her, literally, on a wheel studded with spikes. The wheel shatters at her touch. In the end she is beheaded. That's why paintings show her holding a broken wheel, and often a book. The book matters. Students and philosophers took her as their patron. In her story, the courage comes out of her mind, not instead of it. There's a promise in Luke's gospel that fits her well. Jesus tells his followers that when they are dragged before kings and governors, they shouldn't rehearse their defense. In the Douay-Rheims: "For I will give you a mouth and wisdom." Notice the pairing in Catherine's story. Wisdom without courage stays home and thinks. Courage without wisdom charges in and says something foolish. She is remembered for having both at once: she thought hard, and then she said it out loud, to the one person in the room who could hurt her.
screen: `A LEGEND, HONESTLY TOLD.` · `THE PHILOSOPHERS CHANGE SIDES.` · `A BROKEN WHEEL AND A BOOK.` · `WISDOM AND COURAGE AT ONCE.` · then, large: `FOR I WILL GIVE YOU A MOUTH AND WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think hard about one question. Choose a question that's easy to avoid, the kind that gets pushed away because it's uncomfortable or tangled. Sit with it on purpose. Don't try to solve it in two minutes. Just look at it honestly: what do you actually know, and what are you guessing? If you pray, you can ask for wisdom, and for the courage to act on whatever you find. If you don't, simply let your mind stay with the question without running off. The bell holds the time.
Catherine of Alexandria. The learned young martyr of legend, shown with a book and a broken wheel, patron of students and philosophers.
Your line: wisdom and courage. Today, when you know something true that's awkward to say, think it through first, then say it once, calmly. Day one thousand forty-nine.

1050.title: Andrew (30 November)
1050.hook: the first called, who brought his brother Peter; patron of Scotland and of Constantinople
1050.howItsDone: The feast of Saint Andrew, apostle, is kept on 30 November; it is a great feast in Scotland and for the church of Constantinople, and the season of Advent begins close to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Alexandria. Your line was wisdom and courage. And a week's end, so look back at the company: Rose Philippine Duchesne praying, Mary given as a child, Cecilia singing, Columban on the road, Miguel Pro with open arms, Catherine with her book. Day one thousand fifty.

"Come and see." That's the whole invitation. Two men have been standing with John the Baptist when Jesus walks past, and John points him out. The two men leave John and walk after Jesus, saying nothing yet. Jesus turns and asks what they're looking for. They answer with a question: where do you live? He says, come and see. They spend the rest of the day with him. One of those two men is named in the next verse. Today, Andrew.
screen: `TWO MEN FOLLOW.` → `WHERE DO YOU LIVE?` → `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Look at how John's gospel introduces him. Not as Andrew, the disciple. As "Andrew, the brother of Simon Peter." Even on his big day, he's somebody's brother. And what does he do with his afternoon with Jesus? He goes home. In the Douay-Rheims: "He findeth first his brother Simon, and saith to him: We have found the Messias." Then the verse ends simply: "And he brought him to Jesus." That's Andrew's pattern, and John's gospel shows it more than once. When a huge crowd is hungry, Andrew is the one who points out a boy with five barley loaves and two fishes, even while wondering out loud what good so little could do. When some Greeks come looking for Jesus, they ask Philip, and Philip goes to Andrew, and the two of them bring the request to Jesus. Andrew doesn't give the big speeches. Peter does that. Andrew makes introductions. Eastern Christians give him a title: the First-Called. Tradition says he preached around the Black Sea and was crucified on an X-shaped cross, which is why Scotland, which claims him as patron, flies a white X on blue. The church of Constantinople honors him as its founder, the way Rome honors his brother Peter. In recent times, on Andrew's feast, a delegation from Rome visits the patriarch in Istanbul, and on Peter's feast a delegation from the patriarch visits Rome. The brothers are still bringing people to each other.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be the one who introduces. Settle and breathe. Think of two people you know who don't know each other, but should. Maybe they share a worry, or a hobby, or a hard season. Hold both faces in mind for a while. Picture them meeting, and what they might give each other. If you pray, you can bring both of them to God by name, the way Andrew brought his brother. If you don't, simply decide how you'll make the introduction. The bell holds the time.
